questions.stem: In a law reform inquiry, the terms of reference are:
options: the final recommendations the body gives to the government
the written comments sent to the body by members of the public
the list of laws that parliament has already agreed to change
the matters the body is asked to investigate and report on
questions.explanation: Terms of reference set the scope of an inquiry: what the body must examine and report on. Submissions are the public's written comments, and recommendations come at the end in the final report.

questions.stem: An issues paper published by a law reform commission is best described as a document that:
options: outlines the questions under review and invites public submissions
contains the final recommendations to be given to the Attorney-General
sets out the text of a bill ready to be introduced into parliament
records the judgment of a court on the meaning of an existing law
questions.explanation: An issues paper is released early in an inquiry to explain the issues and ask questions, so that people and groups can make submissions. Final recommendations appear in the report, and bills are drafted by government, not by the commission.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes lobbying from advocacy in law reform?
options: Lobbying happens only in court; advocacy happens only inside parliament
Lobbying is unlawful in Queensland; advocacy is permitted only for registered charities
Lobbying targets decision-makers directly; advocacy is wider public support for a cause
Lobbying is always paid for by government; advocacy is carried out only by courts
questions.explanation: Lobbying is trying to persuade law-makers directly, for example by meeting ministers or members, while advocacy is the broader act of speaking up for a cause or group, including through the media and the public. Both are lawful, and many groups do both.

questions.stem: A law reform commission holds public forums and meets with victims' groups, police and lawyers during an inquiry. This stage is best described as:
options: proclamation
consultation
ratification
codification
questions.explanation: Consultation is the process of seeking the views of the community and stakeholders, often alongside written submissions. Codification is putting law into a single Act, and proclamation is how an Act's commencement may be fixed.

questions.stem: The Australian Law Reform Commission (ALRC) begins an inquiry when:
options: a majority of state parliaments pass motions calling for a review
the Commonwealth Attorney-General refers a matter to it
a member of the public lodges a petition with at least 10,000 signatures
the High Court finds a Commonwealth law invalid and orders a review
questions.explanation: The ALRC is an independent Commonwealth body that inquires into matters referred to it by the Attorney-General, who sets the terms of reference. It cannot begin a full inquiry of its own choosing, and courts do not order it to act.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Queensland Law Reform Commission (QLRC) is correct?
options: It can make binding changes to Queensland law without a vote of parliament
It decides appeals about the meaning of Queensland statutes after trials
It reviews Queensland law, mainly on references from the Attorney-General
It reviews Commonwealth law and reports directly to the Governor-General
questions.explanation: The QLRC, established under the Law Reform Commission Act 1968 (Qld), keeps Queensland law under review and examines branches of law at the Minister's request. Its recommendations are not binding; only parliament can change the law.

questions.stem: In 2018 the QLRC reported on termination of pregnancy laws, and later that year parliament passed the Termination of Pregnancy Act 2018 (Qld). This best shows that a law reform commission:
options: must hold a referendum before its recommendations can take effect
replaces the courts in deciding how the Criminal Code should be applied
can influence reform when parliament chooses to act on its recommendations
has power to repeal sections of the Criminal Code once its report is tabled
questions.explanation: The QLRC was asked to recommend how to modernise and clarify the law, and parliament then legislated, removing abortion offences from the Criminal Code. The commission's influence depended on parliament choosing to act; it has no power to change the law itself.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates law reform commissions as agents of reform?
options: They can overrule parliament, but only on matters of criminal law
They are independent and well researched, but their advice is not binding
Their recommendations are binding, but they can only review laws made in the last ten years
They act quickly on any issue they choose, but they cannot consult the public
questions.explanation: Commissions are independent and consult widely, so their reports are well researched and respected. However, they depend on references from government, inquiries can take years, and parliament may ignore or only partly adopt their recommendations.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes a royal commission from a law reform commission?
options: It can convict people of crimes uncovered during its investigations
It can compel witnesses to attend and give evidence
It is a permanent body that reviews all laws of the state or nation
It is made up only of elected members from both houses of parliament
questions.explanation: Royal commissions are temporary inquiries set up by government with strong powers to require witnesses to attend and documents to be produced. They cannot convict anyone, though they may refer matters for prosecution.

questions.stem: The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (2013-2017) made 409 recommendations. Which Queensland reform best reflects its findings?
options: Lowering of the age of criminal responsibility from 10 years to 8 years
Removal of the right of victims to sue institutions for compensation
Offences of failing to report or protect a child from sexual abuse
Abolition of the Childrens Court and transfer of its work to the District Court
questions.explanation: In 2020 Queensland added offences to the Criminal Code for adults who fail to report a belief that a child sexual offence has been committed and for accountable persons who fail to protect a child. Many jurisdictions also made it easier for survivors to sue institutions.

questions.stem: The Royal Commission into the Child Protection and Youth Detention Systems of the Government of the Northern Territory was set up in 2016 soon after a television program showed the treatment of children in detention. This best shows:
options: a court ordering the government to establish an inquiry into detention
a law reform commission using its own powers to begin an investigation
a referendum approving a new inquiry into the youth justice system
the media prompting a government to establish an inquiry
questions.explanation: The royal commission was announced within days of the ABC's Four Corners program showing footage from the Don Dale Youth Detention Centre. Media coverage created public pressure that led the government to act.

questions.stem: A parliamentary inquiry is best described as an investigation by:
options: a panel of judges into whether a law is constitutionally valid
an independent commission with powers to convict offenders
the Governor into the conduct of ministers and their departments
a committee of members of parliament into a matter referred to it
questions.explanation: Parliamentary committees are made up of members of parliament. In Queensland, portfolio committees inquire into bills and other matters, call for submissions, hold public hearings and report to the Legislative Assembly.

questions.stem: Not Now, Not Ever: Putting an End to Domestic and Family Violence in Queensland (2015) was the report of:
options: a royal commission led by a High Court judge
the Australian Law Reform Commission
a Senate committee of the Commonwealth Parliament
a special taskforce chaired by Dame Quentin Bryce
questions.explanation: The Special Taskforce on Domestic and Family Violence in Queensland, chaired by former Governor-General Dame Quentin Bryce, made 140 recommendations. The government accepted all those directed to it.

questions.stem: After Not Now, Not Ever, Queensland created a specific offence of choking, suffocation or strangulation in a domestic setting (2016). Which statement best evaluates the taskforce as an agent of reform?
options: It replaced parliament's role, because the taskforce drafted and passed the new offence
Its focused inquiry, once accepted by government, led to concrete legal change
It changed the law directly, because taskforce recommendations take effect without legislation
It was ineffective, because its recommendations could only be adopted by the High Court
questions.explanation: A taskforce is set up by government to examine a specific problem and recommend solutions. Its impact depends on government acceptance and parliament legislating, as happened with the strangulation offence in section 315A of the Criminal Code.

questions.stem: Queensland's Women's Safety and Justice Taskforce reported in 2021 on coercive control, and in 2024 parliament created a coercive control offence in the Criminal Code. Which impetus for reform does this best show?
options: A pattern of domestic violence that existing offences did not address
A change in technology that allowed police to collect new types of evidence
A High Court decision that struck down existing domestic violence laws
A treaty obligation that required the state to adopt a federal offence
questions.explanation: Coercive control is a pattern of behaviour that controls and harms a partner, often without a single act that is itself an offence. The taskforce found existing laws focused on single incidents, so parliament created an offence covering a course of conduct.

questions.stem: The Australian Institute of Criminology (AIC) is best described as:
options: a court that hears appeals against criminal sentences
a police force that investigates federal offences
a tribunal that reviews decisions to refuse bail
a Commonwealth research centre on crime and justice
questions.explanation: The AIC is Australia's national research and knowledge centre on crime and justice. It publishes research and data, for example through its National Homicide Monitoring Program. Federal offences are investigated by the Australian Federal Police.

questions.stem: How can the Australian Institute of Criminology most directly influence law reform?
options: By overruling sentences that it considers inconsistent with national averages
By drafting bills and introducing them into the Commonwealth Parliament
By directing state police services to enforce particular offences
By publishing data on crime patterns and costs that law-makers rely on
questions.explanation: The AIC's research shows trends, costs and causes of crime, which governments, law reform bodies and advocacy groups use to justify and design reforms. It has no power to change sentences, introduce bills or direct police.

questions.stem: Raymond Carroll's murder conviction was quashed on appeal in Queensland. He was later convicted of perjury on the same facts, but that conviction was also overturned, and the High Court upheld this in 2002. Which reform did public pressure after the case lead to?
options: Retrial for murder after an acquittal, where there is fresh and compelling evidence
Abolition of trial by jury for murder, with all murder trials heard by a judge alone
Removal of the right to appeal for a person found guilty of murder
A rule that perjury can never be charged after a person gives evidence at trial
questions.explanation: The Carroll case led to calls to reform the double jeopardy rule. In 2007 Queensland amended the Criminal Code to allow the Court of Appeal, on the application of the DPP, to order a retrial for murder if there is fresh and compelling evidence.

questions.stem: In 2017 a national postal survey returned a majority Yes vote, and the Commonwealth Parliament then amended the Marriage Act 1961 to allow same-sex couples to marry. Which impetus for reform is best shown?
options: A technological advance that made earlier laws unworkable
A significant event that created an immediate threat to safety
Changing community values, supported by advocacy and the media
A pattern of crime that existing laws had failed to deter
questions.explanation: Same-sex marriage reform followed a long shift in community attitudes, sustained campaigning by advocacy groups and wide media coverage. The survey result showed majority support and was followed by legislation.

questions.stem: In 2014 Queensland created the offence of unlawful striking causing death, aimed at single-punch assaults, with a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. Which impetus for reform is best shown?
options: A rise in transnational organised crime involving drug imports
A treaty requiring Australia to criminalise acts of terrorism
A pattern of alcohol-fuelled violence and community concern about it
A change in technology allowing crimes to be committed online
questions.explanation: The offence in section 314A of the Criminal Code responded to deaths from single punches, often in nightlife areas, and to campaigns by victims' families. It removed some defences that had made convictions for these deaths difficult.

questions.stem: After a teenager was fatally stabbed, his family campaigned for police to be able to use hand-held metal detectors without a warrant, and parliament legislated 'Jack's Law'. Which agent of reform is best shown?
options: Individuals and lobby groups influencing parliament
The Queensland Law Reform Commission acting on a reference
A royal commission using its coercive powers
A court setting a new precedent on police powers
questions.explanation: Jack's Law, in the Police Powers and Responsibilities Act 2000 (Qld), followed a sustained campaign by the family of Jack Beasley and their foundation. It shows how individuals and lobby groups can persuade a government to change the law.

questions.stem: Section 115A of the Copyright Act 1968 (Cth) allows courts to order internet providers to block overseas websites that infringe copyright. Which impetus for reform does it best show?
options: Patterns of violence in nightlife precincts involving alcohol
Technology making civil wrongs such as digital piracy easier
Changing community values about the right to protest in public places
A significant event involving the use of firearms in a public place
questions.explanation: File-sharing and streaming technology made large-scale copyright infringement easy from overseas, beyond the reach of Australian courts. Site-blocking orders were a legal response to that technological change.

questions.stem: Which reform followed the Port Arthur massacre in Tasmania in 1996?
options: The creation of a national register of all people convicted of sexual offences
The introduction of terrorism offences into the Commonwealth Criminal Code
The abolition of the double jeopardy rule for murder in every state
The National Firearms Agreement, restricting automatic and semi-automatic guns
questions.explanation: Within weeks of the shooting, Commonwealth, state and territory governments agreed to strict uniform gun laws, including bans on automatic and semi-automatic long arms and a buyback. Terrorism offences followed the September 11 attacks of 2001.

questions.stem: The September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001 led the Commonwealth Parliament to create terrorism offences and new powers for security agencies. This best shows which impetus for reform?
options: A change in community values about the rights of accused people
A court decision that left a gap in existing criminal law
A law reform commission recommendation on the use of DNA evidence
A significant event that changed perceptions of risk to the community
questions.explanation: Significant events can quickly change what the community and government see as threats, leading to rapid reform. The anti-terrorism laws were made by parliament in response to the attacks, not on a law reform commission or court's initiative.

questions.stem: Developments in DNA profiling allow police to link suspects to crimes many years later, and laws have been changed to govern how DNA samples are taken and stored. This best shows technology:
options: making existing police powers unnecessary and leading to their repeal
removing the need for courts to decide guilt beyond reasonable doubt
assisting investigations and requiring laws to balance this against privacy
facilitating new crimes that require offences to be created
questions.explanation: Forensic advances help solve crimes but raise questions about consent, privacy and how long samples are kept, so laws must regulate their use. Technology that facilitates crime, such as online fraud, is a different kind of impetus.

questions.stem: Scammers based overseas use fake investment websites to defraud Australians. Which statement best explains why such crime creates pressure for reform?
options: Offenders overseas are hard to reach, so laws and cooperation must adapt
Overseas offenders are automatically tried in Australian courts, so no new law is needed
Online fraud is a civil matter only, so the criminal law cannot respond to it
Victims of fraud have no remedy in Australia unless the offender lives in Queensland
questions.explanation: Transnational and online crime crosses borders, making investigation and prosecution difficult. Reform responses include new offences, regulation of banks and telecommunications providers, and international agreements on sharing evidence and extradition.

questions.stem: Which body was established under the Law Reform Commission Act 1968 (Qld)?
options: The Crime and Corruption Commission
The Queensland Human Rights Commission
The Queensland Law Reform Commission
The Australian Law Reform Commission
questions.explanation: The QLRC is Queensland's standing law reform body, set up by the 1968 Act. The ALRC is a Commonwealth body under the Australian Law Reform Commission Act 1996 (Cth).

questions.stem: Which term describes a group that tries to persuade members of parliament to change the law in its members' interests?
options: A royal commission
A portfolio committee
A law reform commission
A lobby group
questions.explanation: Lobby groups, also called pressure or interest groups, try to influence law-makers directly for a cause or their members. Royal commissions, committees and law reform commissions are official bodies set up by government or parliament.

questions.stem: A royal commission is established by:
options: the Australian Institute of Criminology, using its data
the executive government, which sets its terms of reference
the High Court, after a case reveals a problem in the law
a petition signed by a majority of voters in the state
questions.explanation: Royal commissions are set up by the executive government (formally by the Governor-General or a Governor) with terms of reference that define their task. Courts and research bodies cannot establish them.

questions.stem: A reform to restrict gambling advertising is opposed by people who say adults should make their own choices without government interference. This criticism is often called:
options: the 'separation of powers' argument
the 'double jeopardy' argument
the 'standing' argument
the 'nanny state' argument
questions.explanation: The 'nanny state' criticism argues that some laws are paternalistic and restrict personal freedom too much. It can be a barrier to reforms such as restrictions on alcohol, gambling or risky behaviour.

questions.stem: A law reform commission recommends a statewide program of specialist courts, but the government declines because of the cost. Which barrier to reform is shown?
options: Social divisions
Judicial conservatism
Lack of standing
Budgetary constraints
questions.explanation: Governments must fund reforms from limited budgets, so expensive recommendations may be delayed or rejected even when supported. Social divisions refer to the community being split on the issue.

questions.stem: A proposed reform deeply divides the community, and the government fears losing marginal seats at the next election. Which statement best evaluates these barriers?
options: They prevent reform permanently, because only courts can change divisive laws
They apply only to Commonwealth laws, because state governments face no elections
Political pressure and social division can delay reform even when evidence supports it
They have little effect, because governments must implement every inquiry's recommendations
questions.explanation: Members of parliament are accountable to voters, so they may avoid divisive reforms or wait for clearer public support. This can make law slow to respond to evidence, though it also keeps law-making connected to community values.

questions.stem: A student argues that laws should change as soon as a high-profile crime causes public outrage. Which is the strongest counter-argument?
options: Public outrage cannot influence parliament because voting is compulsory
Only the High Court can change criminal laws in response to events
Hasty reform may be poorly researched and have unintended effects
Parliament has no power to change criminal laws without a referendum
questions.explanation: Reform driven by a single event can be rushed, poorly targeted or harsher than needed, which is why inquiries and consultation are valued. Significant events do legitimately prompt reform, but the evidence should guide its design.

questions.stem: A student recommends a new law requiring online platforms to remove cyberstalking content within 24 hours. Which pair of legal criteria would best justify this recommendation?
options: It avoids all costs and requires no change to any existing law
It applies only in Queensland and so cannot conflict with any law
It protects victims' safety and can be enforced against the platforms
It is the oldest approach and was proposed by the youngest members
questions.explanation: Recommendations are justified using criteria such as whether the law protects rights, achieves just outcomes, is enforceable and is acceptable to the community. Saying a law has no costs or conflicts at all is rarely accurate and is not a legal criterion.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why a parliamentary inquiry may be preferred to a royal commission for some law reform issues?
options: Its recommendations must be implemented by the government in full
It is usually cheaper and quicker, and members are close to law-making
It has stronger coercive powers and can compel any person to give evidence
It is completely independent of government and political parties
questions.explanation: Parliamentary committees cost less than royal commissions and members can carry findings into debate. However, they are made up of politicians, so party interests can affect their work, and governments need not adopt their recommendations.

questions.stem: A submission to a law reform inquiry is:
options: the official order from the Governor that formally begins the inquiry
the final decision of parliament on whether to accept the inquiry's report
a court document that starts a civil action against the government
a written response from a person or group giving their views on the issues
questions.explanation: Inquiries invite submissions from the public, experts and organisations so that a wide range of views and evidence is considered. Submissions are often published unless confidentiality is requested.

questions.stem: A student compares the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse with the QLRC. Which comparison is most accurate?
options: Both are permanent bodies that review all Commonwealth and state laws continuously
Both can make binding changes to the law without parliament passing legislation
The royal commission could compel evidence; the QLRC relies on research and consultation
The QLRC could compel evidence; the royal commission relies only on public submissions
questions.explanation: A royal commission is a temporary inquiry with coercive powers to compel witnesses and documents, which suited uncovering abuse hidden within institutions. The QLRC is a standing body that reviews the law through research, papers and submissions. Neither can change the law itself.

questions.stem: Victims' groups want tougher bail laws, while legal aid lawyers warn that more accused people will be remanded before trial. What does this tension best illustrate about law reform?
options: Reform of bail laws is a Commonwealth matter, so state groups have no influence
Reform must balance safety against the presumption of innocence
Reform can only occur when every interest group agrees on the proposed change
Reform is decided by courts, which weigh the views of interest groups in each case
questions.explanation: Many reforms involve competing rights and interests, and law-makers must weigh them. Here community safety and victims' concerns compete with the presumption of innocence and the cost of remand. Unanimous agreement is not required.
